config.title: Optimistic UI

intro.title: Optimistic UI
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a simple React app that updates a like counter instantly when a user clicks a button, simulating a fast and responsive user experience. You'll learn the concept of Optimistic UI, which means showing the expected result immediately before the server confirms the action, making your app feel faster. The main technologies involved are React state with the useState hook and event handlers to manage the UI updates. This approach is commonly used in social media apps for actions like liking posts or sending messages.
intro.usecase: Optimistic UI is essential for creating responsive interfaces that feel instantaneous to users. You'll see this pattern in social media platforms when users like posts, in e-commerce sites when adding items to carts, and in collaborative tools when editing documents. As a React developer, implementing optimistic updates improves perceived performance in forms, dashboards, and interactive panels where immediate feedback matters more than waiting for server confirmation. This approach transforms clunky interfaces into smooth experiences that keep users engaged.

objectives: Initialize and manage optimistic state in a React component
Implement UI updates that reflect optimistic changes before server confirmation
Configure fallback logic to revert optimistic updates when server requests fail
Integrate optimistic state with asynchronous API calls in event handlers
Construct user interfaces that provide immediate visual feedback for user actions
Manipulate component state to maintain consistency between optimistic and actual data
Apply optimistic UI patterns to common interactive elements like forms and buttons

steps.title: Create the main component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named TaskList that returns an empty div element.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Make sure to export the component.
steps.expectedOutcome: A TaskList component is defined and exported, returning an empty div.
successCriteria: TaskList component is created as a functional component and returns an empty div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the component returns an empty div element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Check that you've defined a functional component named TaskList that returns an empty div.

steps.title: Initialize state for tasks
steps.instruction: Inside the TaskList component, use useState to create a state variable called 'tasks' initialized with an array of task objects. Each task should have id, text, and completed properties.
steps.hint: Call useState with an initial array containing at least one task object. Example: { id: 1, text: 'Learn React', completed: false }
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a 'tasks' state variable initialized with an array of task objects, each containing id, text, and completed properties.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with an initial array containing at least one task object that has id, text, and completed properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've initialized state, but make sure the initial value is an array of objects with id, text, and completed properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The tasks state isn't properly initialized. Use useState with an array of task objects containing id, text, and completed.

steps.title: Define the addTask handler
steps.instruction: Inside the TaskList component, define a function named addTask that takes newTaskText as a parameter. The function should create a new task object with id and text properties,
steps.hint: Create a function that receives newTaskText, generates a unique id (you can use Date.now() for simplicity), creates a task object, and updates state using the setTasks function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has an addTask function that can create new task objects and update the tasks state.
successCriteria: A function named addTask is defined inside the TaskList component, it takes newTaskText as a parameter, creates a task object with id and text properties, and updates the tasks state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your addTask function takes newTaskText as a parameter, creates a complete task object with both id and text properties, and properly updates the tasks state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The addTask function isn't defined correctly. It should be a function inside TaskList that takes newTaskText, creates a task object, and updates the tasks state.

steps.title: Define the toggleTask handler
steps.instruction: Inside your TaskList component, define a function named toggleTask that takes a taskId parameter and updates the tasks state by toggling the completed property of the matching task.
steps.hint: Use setTasks with a callback function that maps over the current tasks array. For each task, check if its id matches the taskId parameter and toggle its completed property if it does.
steps.expectedOutcome: A toggleTask function is defined inside the TaskList component that properly toggles the completed status of a task by its id.
successCriteria: The toggleTask function is defined, takes a taskId parameter, and uses setTasks with a callback that maps over tasks to toggle the matching task's completed property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your toggleTask function properly toggles the completed property for the matching task id. Make sure you're using the setTasks callback pattern.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggleTask function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function that takes taskId as a parameter and updates the tasks state by toggling the completed property of the task with that id.

steps.title: Add the task list structure
steps.instruction: Inside your TaskList component, return JSX that includes an h1 heading with the text 'Task List' and an unordered list element.
steps.hint: The return statement should contain a fragment or a div wrapper with the heading and ul.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a basic structure with a heading and an empty list container.
successCriteria: The component returns JSX containing an h1 with 'Task List' and a ul element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have both an h1 with 'Task List' and a ul element in the returned JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The structure is missing. Ensure your component returns JSX with an h1 and ul.

steps.title: Display tasks in the list
steps.instruction: Inside the unordered list, map over the tasks state to render each task as a list item showing the task text and a visual indicator of its completed status.
steps.hint: Use the map method on the tasks array. For each task, return a list item (<li>) that displays the task's text and completion status.
steps.expectedOutcome: The task list will display each task's text and a visual indicator (like a checkmark or text) showing whether it's completed.
successCriteria: The unordered list contains a map over the tasks state that renders list items with task text and completion status.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're mapping over the tasks state and rendering each task's text and completion status.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to use the map method on the tasks array inside the unordered list to render each task.

steps.title: Add the toggle button and wire its onClick
steps.instruction: Inside the task mapping in your return statement, add a button element with the text 'Toggle' and wire its onClick event to call toggleTask with the current task's id.
steps.hint: Place the button inside the <li> element, after the task text. Use onClick={() => toggleTask(task.id)} to call the handler with the specific task id.
steps.expectedOutcome: Each task item in the list will now have a 'Toggle' button next to it that, when clicked, will toggle the task's completion status.
successCriteria: A button with text 'Toggle' is added inside each <li> element, and its onClick handler calls toggleTask with the current task's id.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added a button with the text 'Toggle' and wired its onClick to call toggleTask with the specific task id.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the task mapping, add a button element with the text 'Toggle' and set its onClick to call toggleTask with task.id.

steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will now have an input field and an 'Add Task' button positioned above the task list heading.
successCriteria: An <input> element and a <button> with text 'Add Task' are added inside the <div> before the <h1>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some UI elements, but make sure you have both an <input> and a <button> with the text 'Add Task' placed before the <h1> element.
